# The Importance of Studying the Implementation of Cancer Data Standards

**Authors:** Travis J. Osterman; Jiarong Ye

**Affiliations:** 1.Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN | 2.Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN

## Abstract

Data standards promise better quality measurement, discovery, population health management and interoperability. For oncology practices to make informed decisions about implementation, it is paramount that the cancer informatics community continue to study and publish diverse methods to structure data.

Terminologies such as the International Classification of Disease (ICD)1, Current Procedural Terminology (CPT®)2 and Systematized Medical Nomenclature for Medicine–Clinical Terminology (SNOMED CT)3 are ubiquitous in medical practice and serve various purposes including patient care, research and billing. Cancer data standards like United States Core Data for Interoperability+ Cancer (USCDI+ Cancer)4 and the minimal Common Oncology Data Elements (mCODE™)5 utilize these terminologies to facilitate interoperable health information exchange among electronic health records (EHR). These standards are not static; they evolve over time to align with the evolving needs of oncology practice6. A key challenge in developing cancer data standards has been determining who will structure the data. A form with a thousand fields may comprehensively describe a patient encounter, but it’s not practical for clinical use. The promise of interoperable cancer data standards lies in their seamless integration into the oncologist’s workflow. Various methods have been explored to achieve the dual goals of structuring data and supporting efficient clinical workflows. This remains a key topic in the field of cancer informatics.

Tevaarwerk, et al. implement and study structuring of five mCODE categories into the EHR at The Mayo Clinic7. Implementation studies such as this are critical to inform the evolution of cancer data standards. This study chose to implement the structured data capture within the clinical note. Similar methods have been reported for successfully collecting Commission on Cancer metrics for patients undergoing breast surgery8. This method embeds semi-structured data structures within the note and typically allows users to choose from a preselected set of options. For instance, Eastern Cooperative Group (ECOG) performance status would map to zero through five. This appears as text in the rendered note but also saved discretely separately from the note. This allows future researchers to study, for example, the safety of chemotherapy administration to patients with a given performance status. Tevaarwerk showed this data collection method within the clinical note improved structured data collection without increasing time spent in the EHR. Specifically, the capture of discrete staging doubled from 32% to 64% following the intervention.

In contrast, a study by Emamekhoo et al. at the University of Wisconsin achieved structured cancer staging of 90% by implementing a Close Visit Validation that prevented a clinic visit from being completed without finishing a staging form9. The staging form was not part of the clinical note and described an alternative strategy to collect discrete data from the clinical visits.

Another popular approach is to allow oncologists to write a traditional note. The note text is later parsed using natural language processing (NLP). Dr. Odisho et al. at the University of California, San Franciso, showed NLP to be an effective strategy for structuring prostate cancer pathology data such as Gleason score10. Similar studies have used NLP to extract the rationale for cancer treatment discontinuation successfully11. The appeal of such systems is tempting. The oncologist may write a note in whatever format or style she chooses, and the NLP engine will read and extract all relevant data elements. Several challenges exist with NLP, however. First, studying the accuracy of these implementations tends to be costly. NLP accuracy is often compared against a gold standard clinic review, which can be time-consuming. Second, validation is necessary to maintain system performance if the NLP pipeline is used at another oncology practice where the types of clinical documentation may differ substantially. Finally, introducing systems such as new note templates, dictation, or ambient voice transcription that change the format of notes may negatively impact performance.

Large language models (LLM) such as Llama, ChatGPT and Gemini have been the latest promise to support traditional clinical notes like NLP while addressing many challenges. One recent example is mCODEGPT, which used an LLM to structure clinical notes with 95% data element accuracy12. Additionally, Choi, et al. were able to use a ChatGPT-based model to extract and standardize data from pathology reports nearly 3,000 patients with an overall accuracy of 87% for a cost of 95.40 USD13.These systems are the natural evolution of NLP pipelines. One key difference with using LLMs to structure clinical data is that external validation and migration to dictation or new note templates are less likely to impact the results dramatically. Large language models are better suited to parse various data formats and styles. For instance, embedded tabular data, such as a table with laboratory values, is likely better understood by an LLM.

NLP and LLMs will likely continue to share the same challenge: evaluation requires a cost gold standard review by clinical experts. Dr. Tevaarwerk et al. describe an appropriate middle ground for oncology practices that see the importance of collecting discrete structured data. Incorporating the data collection into the clinical note provides less workflow impact than forcing the oncologist to complete a separate synoptic staging form. Multiple SmartPhrases™ can be incorporated into a note and do not require the entire note to be a single template, which helps support multidisciplinary care.

The future promises an ambient scribe system that can listen to a discussion between an oncologist and patient, understand which data to include, format, and write the note, and then have all the data available discretely for quality reporting, discovery, and other uses is appealing. In that world, the oncologist can focus on patient care with transparent documentation in the background.

Until we have idealized documentation in oncology, oncology practices must share how they implement cancer data standards such as mCODE and USCDI+ Cancer. Sharing implementation experiences helps inform the data standard maintainers on remaining gaps and challenges. Additionally, practices can make more informed decisions on their local approach to structuring data.
